ELI5: Why does Wikipedia insist on using secondary sources in its articles?

You know the old saying "there's two sides to every story"? That's a folksy way of saying primary sources are very rarely free of bias. If I want to know how big the fish you caught really was, a photo someone took of you holding it (a secondary source) is going to be more reliable than your telling of the story.

However, there is a major problem. If I took a photo holding it (a primary source) only the person who told a story about the picture makes it counts (it has become a secondary source).

This creates huge problems. A citizen of a town can't write about the town because they are a primary source, but someone thousands of miles away can write outdated information. People can't correct very incorrect information about their own lives unless they use a work around and even authors are told that they aren't credible sources for their own books.

I'm not necessarily defending the policy, because you make valid points, but I do think what I said is the spirit in which it was implemented.

Now, if we want an ELI5 on why they don't allow exceptions in specific situations where a primary source might be credible, that's "because the types of personalities that desire to write encyclopedias trend towards the pedantic-asshole-bureaucrat end of the spectrum, and the ability to strike down other people's contributions for failing to meet a mostly-arbitrarily-established standard gives their small lives a sense of purpose", but that probably runs afoul of guideline 1.1 that says to avoid being needlessly hostile.
